SEC-H8-01.note: Agrees with key. Head 'The two deepest cores' is plural and sits at the sentence opening; the comma-opened appositive must close with a comma, so a mismatched dash is a real error under any style. Four words after the blank ('the sequence of ash layers') resolve nothing - clean on that test. Downgraded from hard because neither axis requires the other: the head is the first noun phrase you read and 'cores ... contradict' is audible, and the mark-matching half is mechanical once you notice the opening comma. Explanation is accurate.

SEC-H8-02.note: Agrees with key. 'containing:' is double-wrong and dies on sight, so the live field is three, not four. Four words after ('larch resin, walnut oil,') do not resolve: the bare list is compatible with both 'contained' and 'contained:'. The colon-between-verb-and-object rule is real (Chicago 6.61) and the explanation states it correctly. Medium: the two axes are independent, and the key is the plainest option in the set, which is the heuristic that wins across most of this batch.

SEC-H8-03.note: Agrees with key. Closest call in the batch: '; the night assistant photographed' is defensible on the standard principle that the past perfect is optional where an adverbial ('three nights earlier') already fixes anteriority. What defeats that defense is the coordinate 'and had told nobody outside the dome' sharing the same subject - you cannot coordinate 'photographed ... and had told'. So exclusive holds, but on the coordination, not on the sequence rule the explanation leads with. Note that same trailing 'had told' also hands the tense axis to a solver who never reasons about sequence at all; it is ~20 words after the blank, so outside the four-word window but functionally the same shortcut.

SEC-H8-04.note: Agrees with key. Four words after ('twice over, so that') resolve nothing. But the explanation overstates its rule: 'a comma does not separate the halves of a compound predicate' is not absolute - Chicago 6.23 permits the comma where it is needed for clarity or emphasis. Here it is not needed and the predicates are short, so the key survives and I did not spend a false; flagging it because this is the same species of over-absolute rule statement the two ACT English items were dropped on today. Second axis is spoon-fed: a dedicated preceding sentence exists only to say there were four coopers, so the possessive costs no reasoning.

SEC-H8-05.note: Agrees with key. Subject-verb comma is a hard error (unlike the compound-predicate comma in 04/21), so this axis is genuinely exclusive. Four words after ('two localities that no') do not resolve - the object's own number is inert. Plural head 'The sheets' opens the sentence; the singular decoys ('transect', 'student', 'gazetteer') are well placed but the head is never out of sight. One of three items (05/18/22) on the plural-head-across-modifier template.

SEC-H8-06.note: Agrees with key, but this is a ONE-rule item wearing a two-rule subskill line. The batch's own explanation concedes it: the indicative forms are wrong 'for that reason alone', so the agreement half is never load-bearing and 'every copy' only decides which wrong answer a solver who misses the subjunctive lands on. The trigger 'demanded that' sits ~12 words BEFORE the blank and decides everything by itself; nothing in the four words after ('to the clerk of') matters. 'were delivered' is a dead option. Does not meet the two-interacting-rules bar.

SEC-H8-07.note: Agrees with key. SHORTCUT, and it is upstream rather than downstream: the matrix verb 'does not list' stands in the same sentence before the blank and is already singular, so the agreement axis is handed over without ever locating the head or discounting 'two appraisers'. Only the finiteness axis does work. Four words after ('the press, the frames') resolve nothing. One strained defense for 'but record' - reading it as a bare infinitive coordinated under 'does' ('does not list X but record Y') - but that negates the whole coordination and is not the available reading, so exclusive stands. Minor: serial comma was dropped here while item 22 used it; a revision of the batch written after this grade added it, so that point is already settled.

SEC-H8-08.note: Agrees with key, and this is one of the two or three items that actually earns the hard label: both axes are live, neither is resolved by a nearby cue, and each distractor is correct on one axis. 'has asked for' before the blank is singular but belongs to the relative clause ('every reviewer'), so it does not leak the matrix number. Four words after ('the samples from the') resolve nothing; the parallel 'and to publish' is ~12 words downstream. Shares its subject frame 'The one thing ...' verbatim with item 13.

SEC-H8-09.note: Agrees with key. Clean 2x2, each distractor right on exactly one axis, and the since-clause genuinely bars the simple past. Four words after ('in a crate beneath') resolve nothing; 'since the port authority was dissolved' is ~13 words downstream, outside the window. Medium rather than hard only because both cues are audible: plural head opens the sentence and 'since' is a drilled present-perfect trigger.

SEC-H8-10.note: Agrees with key. The supplement carries commas of its own, so the dash close is doubly required and the explanation is right about why. Four words after ('now beyond reconstruction, and') resolve nothing. Medium: 'The drum record ... is' is the plainest possible agreement once the supplement is bracketed off, and bracketing is exactly what the opening dash tells you to do, so the two rules assist each other rather than interacting.

SEC-H8-11.note: Agrees with key. 'By the time X arrived' is an anteriority frame that requires the past perfect, and the fronted clause is long enough that the comma is mandatory, not optional - both halves hold. Four words after ('the whole of the') resolve nothing. Two sentences of setup (alum supplier, unfamiliar flock) are inert filler that no axis uses. Same past-perfect template as 03 and 23.

SEC-H8-12.note: Agrees with key. Definite past adverbial bars the present perfect; singular head 'The row' across a plural-stuffed relative clause. Four words after ('to its full depth') do not resolve, but the tense-deciding adverbial 'in the single season' begins at word five - just outside the window and worth watching. DEFECT IN THE PASSAGE, not the item: 'a yard capacity is fixed less by its labor' needs 'a yard's capacity' - read as an attributive noun the following 'its' has no antecedent. A revision of the batch written after this grade fixed it to "a yard's capacity"; recorded here because the grade was taken before that.

SEC-H8-13.note: Agrees with key. Clause before the colon is independent and the colon delivers what it promises; the comma variants leave the how-clause hanging. Four words after ('the crucibles were charged') resolve nothing. Medium: the singular head 'The one thing' is the same frame as item 08, and by the second appearance the agreement axis is free. 'at all' at the end of the sentence reads slightly off but is not an error.

SEC-H8-14.note: Agrees with key. Four words after ('tallies by more than') resolve nothing - the plural 'tallies' is the possessed noun and says nothing about the possessor's number. But the possessive axis is spoon-fed by a planted sentence ('Four districts lay along the river, and each was walked by its own enumerator') exactly as in 04, so the item reduces to the mark-matching rule plus a lookup. Third of the three items (01/14/24) built on comma-opened-supplement.

SEC-H8-15.note: Agrees with key. The perfect-infinitive contrast is the subtlest single distinction in the batch and would carry a hard rating on its own; the parallelism half is easy enough to drag it back to medium. Four words after ('it with whatever the') resolve nothing; 'in the following spring' is ~10 words downstream and is what decides the aspect axis. 'and restocking' / 'and having restocked' are both non-parallel and die together, so the live field is three.

SEC-H8-16.note: KEY IS RIGHT BUT THE ITEM IS BROKEN BY THE RECORDED SHORTCUT, and it is the worst case in the batch. The three words immediately after the blank are 'the whole stack'. Both passive options then read 'the stack was moved the whole stack to the lee of the barn' and 'the stack has been moved the whole stack ...' - ungrammatical on transitivity alone. A solver kills half the field without reading the introductory participial phrase, which is the rule the item is built to test; the dangling-modifier axis is never exercised. What remains is a bare simple-past-vs-present-perfect call decided by 'in the spring of that year'. Rewrite so the post-blank object cannot discriminate voice, or the headline rule is untested.

SEC-H8-17.note: Agrees with key. Four words after ('the state of the') resolve nothing. ', he recording' is wrong on both axes and is a dead option, so the live field is three and the item collapses to the comma-splice rule, which is the most basic boundary rule on the test. Toward the easy end of medium. The natural writer's fix here would be a comma-less compound predicate ('and recorded'), which is not offered - not a defect, but it makes the semicolon feel imposed rather than required.

SEC-H8-18.note: Agrees with key. Four words after ('the line by something') resolve nothing. Both axes hold: the sentence has no other predicate, and 'The levels' is plural. 'raising' and 'having raised' are near-duplicates of each other and die on the same step, so the real choice is 'raise' vs 'raises'. Third instance of the plural-head-across-modifier template (05/18/22). Present-tense 'raise' for a historical survey error is defensible as a persisting fact.

SEC-H8-19.note: Agrees with key. The absolute-phrase construction is the least commonly drilled thing in the batch, which argues for hard; what pulls it back is that the two words right after the blank ('the men') announce a new subject and therefore a mandatory boundary, killing both comma-less options before any analysis. That is the four-word-window defect again, in its milder form - here the shortcut is inherent to a boundary rule rather than accidental, but it still means only the finite-vs-participle axis does work. 'The mold had cooled overnight,' is a strong splice distractor.

SEC-H8-20.note: Agrees with key. Dash close required, and doubly so because the supplement carries an internal comma - a closing comma would read as one more list item, as the explanation correctly says. WATCH THE WINDOW: 'in a single winter' begins at word two after the blank and settles the tense axis by itself ('down'/'in'/'a'/'single'), so the definite-past-interval half is decided inside the four-word window. The mark axis is untouched by it, so the item survives; it is the narrowest escape in the batch. Number is deliberately not an axis here, which is welcome variety.

SEC-H8-21.note: Agrees with key. Same upstream leak as item 07 and more blatant: 'lists' sits immediately before the blank, already singular, so the agreement axis is resolved by the adjacent word and the long relative clause about 'the two assayers' never has to be discounted. Only the comma axis does work. Four words after ('the weight after cupellation') resolve nothing. Same Chicago 6.23 caveat as 04 - the explanation's 'no comma stands before the conjunction in a compound predicate' is a default, not an absolute - and the same conclusion: the comma is not needed for clarity here, so the key stands.

SEC-H8-22.note: Agrees with key. Four words after ('the hour of every') resolve nothing, but the number axis is confirmed twice downstream in the same sentence by 'they' and by the plural 'note' in 'they never once note the weather' - the explanation openly leans on the pronoun. 'gives:' is wrong on both axes and dead. So the live choice is 'give' vs 'give:', i.e. the colon rule alone, already tested in item 02. Medium.

SEC-H8-23.note: Agrees with key. 'by the date of the earliest trench' requires the perfect, and the that-clause requires a finite verb; 'having reached' and 'reaching' die together. Four words after ('the base of the') resolve nothing; the parallel 'had been waterlogged' is far downstream and corroborates the tense. 'reached' is a strong distractor. Same anteriority template as 03 and 11 - three items, and solving any one gives the rule for the other two.

SEC-H8-24.note: Agrees with key. Comma-opened supplement closes with a comma; the interval is shut at both ends (1688 to the closure), so the present perfect is barred. Four words after ('by about a third') resolve nothing; 'across those four decades' at words five to eight is the tense resolver, just outside the window. Number is correctly not an axis. Medium, and the third sighting of the comma-supplement rule (01/14/24), by which point it costs nothing.
